references.text: God sends Moses to Pharaoh to lead the people of Israel out of Egypt, which is the mission now being carried out.
God instructs Moses and the elders of Israel to ask Pharaoh to let them travel three days into the wilderness to offer sacrifices to the Lord.
God gives Moses the message to demand that Pharaoh release the people of Israel, referred to as God's firstborn son.
Repetition of the demand 'Let my people go, so they may serve me in the wilderness' with the formula 'Thus says the Lord'.
The same demand is repeated to Pharaoh: 'Let my people go, so they may serve me'.
Moses again conveys the Lord's command to let the people go to serve Him.
The Lord sends Moses to Pharaoh with the message 'Let my people go, so they may serve me'.
Moses and Aaron confront Pharaoh with the question of how long he will refuse to humble himself and let the people go.
Moses explains that they must leave to hold a feast for the Lord.
The letter to the Hebrews refers to Moses' faith when he left Egypt without fearing the king's anger.
The constant in God's will: Confirms that the demand for liberation remains unchanged even after the first rejection.
Contrast in the demand: God's call for total freedom versus Pharaoh's willingness to compromise with limited conditions.
Repetition as theological emphasis: Affirms that God's plan is unshakable through all the plagues.
Human compromise: Pharaoh copies God's words but limits freedom, revealing his lack of true submission.
Continuity in the message: No matter how severe the plague becomes, God's demand for liberation remains the same.
Pharaoh's resistance mechanisms: Shows how Pharaoh attempts to limit liberation even when he partially acknowledges God's demands.
Conflict over place and freedom: God's demand to go to the wilderness versus Pharaoh's desire to keep the people in Egypt.
Consequence of the confrontation: Shows how God's judgments lead to a temporary recognition of sin in Pharaoh.
